routes.description: Establish God through convergent metaphysical, causal, teleological, moral, and interpersonal grounds extending beyond dependent nature.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if observed reality requires an ultimate actual and intelligent source properly identifiable as God and moral or interpersonal evidence independently supports that conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined natural-theology and moral-law inferences warrant affirming that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Show that change, causation, and contingency require a nondependent source of actuality rather than an infinite instrumental regress.
Show that natural order, universals, or sufficient explanation require an intellect or necessary ground beyond nature.
Show that objective moral obligations exist beyond human opinion and require grounding in a divine intellect.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend inference from natural effects to extranatural causes as continuous with explanatory reasoning used in science.
Account for interpersonal knowledge of God that is not reducible to scientific testing alone.

routes.description: Withhold belief unless the affirmative supplies a defined, coherent, evidentially supported God conclusion and closes the gap from proposed causes to classical theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative inferences remain unsupported, underdetermined, or unnecessary, or if a capable God expected to be evident remains insufficiently disclosed.

motionBridge.description: Show that the presented arguments and evidence do not meet the burden required to affirm that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Require the affirmative claimant to define God and provide a valid, supported demonstration rather than shift the burden to disbelief.
Show that first-cause or explanatory premises do not establish a divine mind, classical attributes, or coherent atemporal agency.
Show that unresolved natural models and cosmic ignorance do not license an undemonstrated supernatural explanatory candidate.
Show that moral assessments can be objective relative to human goals without establishing an independently existing divine moral law.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require verifiable disclosure from any capable personal God who wants human beings to know that God exists.
Maintain a tentative conclusion that remains open to revision upon a valid argument supported by evidence.

sectionSelections.title: Metaphysical inference and the burden of proof
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue governs whether dependent features of reality warrant the God conclusion and what evidential burden that affirmative conclusion must satisfy.

proSelections.proposition: Chains of potential or dependent causes require an actual and necessary source beyond the chain, identified as God.
Essence and existence, relational unity, universals, and the demand for ultimate explanation point to a divine intellect beyond nature.

conSelections.proposition: The God claimant bears the burden of proof, and inability to disprove an undefined or unfalsifiable God does not justify belief.
Finite observers cannot establish maximal divine attributes or infer from a powerful being to the creator, sustainer, and moral foundation of classical theism.

sectionSelections.title: First cause, regress, and atemporal causation
sectionSelections.rationale: The coherence and reach of the Thomistic causal series determine whether change within nature requires a purely actual first mover outside time.

proSelections.proposition: An instrumental series moving potency to actuality cannot regress infinitely and therefore requires a purely actual first mover identified as God.
Thomistic causation can be simultaneous rather than temporal, while an infinite series of mere potencies cannot actualize anything.

conSelections.proposition: Observed causal regularities within the universe cannot simply be projected beyond its accessible history, and timeless existence has not been coherently demonstrated.
A first-cause model does not establish God or a mind, does not explain atemporal causation, and need not treat descriptive natural laws as products of a lawgiver.

sectionSelections.title: Scientific explanation and supernatural causes
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue determines whether natural observations can place supernatural entities among legitimate explanatory candidates or whether the inference exceeds scientific method.

proSelections.proposition: Natural observations used in cosmological and Thomistic arguments point toward a supernatural creator, first cause, necessary being, or designer.
Aquinas's Five Ways are scientific inductive arguments insofar as they organize observations of nature into inferences to the best explanation.

conSelections.proposition: Explanatory inference cannot admit an undemonstrated supernatural candidate, and ignorance about cosmic origins does not make such a cause plausible or true.
Methodological naturalism restricts scientific explanations to demonstrable natural causes rather than undetectable supernatural entities.

sectionSelections.title: Objective morality and divine grounding
sectionSelections.rationale: The moral-law route depends on whether objective wrongness exists beyond human attitudes and whether such objectivity requires a divine intellect rather than stipulated human goals.

proSelections.proposition: Objective right and wrong extend beyond individual opinion and therefore require moral law grounded in a divine intellect.
The existence of acts that are wrong independently of human opinion points to objective moral law and therefore to a divine intellect.

conSelections.proposition: Moral judgments assess actions and intentions against human goals and well-being without requiring an externally caused law of nature.
Once morality is grounded in the well-being of thinking creatures, objective physical facts permit moral assessments without a universal divine law.

sectionSelections.title: Natural signs, hiddenness, and interpersonal knowledge
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue addresses whether apparent order or personal acquaintance supplies knowledge of God despite the skeptical demand for public and verifiable divine disclosure.

proSelections.proposition: Consistent goal-directed behavior by mindless natural objects implies that an intelligent mind guides natural regularities.
Knowledge of God is interpersonal and can transcend scientific proof, as direct knowledge of love in close relationships can do.

conSelections.proposition: A capable God who wants belief should provide detectable evidence, yet alleged revelations remain unverifiable or insufficient.
Claims about natural theology, supernatural science, objective morality, and private relationship do not demonstrate God's existence or answer divine hiddenness.
